cards.explanation: The answer is many foreign women. Solomon, Israel's king, had every kind of treasure, and the text still points at his heart: “King Solomon, however, loved many foreign women along with the daughter of Pharaoh…” (1 Kings 11:1). That little “however” turns the whole story, friends.

The word is intermarry. The LORD had told the Israelites, “You must not intermarry with them, for surely they will turn your hearts after their gods.” (1 Kings 11:2). It was a warning with the reason attached. When the LORD tells you something, friends, He isn't hiding the ball.

The answer is True, and the LORD said it plainly. “You must not intermarry with them, for surely they will turn your hearts after their gods.” (1 Kings 11:2). That word “surely” is not a maybe. And the same verse says, “Yet Solomon clung to these women in love.”

The answer is David. Verse 4 says Solomon, Israel's king, “…was not wholeheartedly devoted to the LORD his God, as his father David had been.” Same house and same family, but his heart went a different direction. That's why the text sets father and son side by side, friends.

The answer is that he did evil in the sight of the LORD, and the text doesn't soften it. “So Solomon did evil in the sight of the LORD; unlike his father David, he did not follow the LORD completely.” (1 Kings 11:6). Solomon, Israel's king, had followed Ashtoreth and Milcom right before this. I think this is a heavy verse to read, friends.

The answer is a high place for gods of Moab and Ammon. Solomon, Israel's king, “…built a high place for Chemosh the abomination of Moab and for Molech the abomination of the Ammonites.” (1 Kings 11:7). It went up on a hill east of Jerusalem.

The answer is False, friends. After Solomon, Israel's king, built the high place for Chemosh and Molech, the text says, “He did the same for all his foreign wives, who burned incense and sacrificed to their gods.” (1 Kings 11:8). The phrase “…all his foreign wives…” is the giveaway.

The answer is that his heart had turned away from the LORD. That's the reason the text gives. “Now the LORD grew angry with Solomon, because his heart had turned away from the LORD, the God of Israel, who had appeared to him twice.” (1 Kings 11:9). Solomon was Israel's king, and the LORD had appeared to him twice. I think that makes the turning even heavier.
The answer is twice. The LORD, the God of Israel, “…had appeared to him twice.” (1 Kings 11:9). That's Solomon, Israel's king. The text gives the exact count, friends, so there's no guessing needed.

The answer is kingdom. The LORD said, “Because you have done this and have not kept My covenant and My statutes, which I have commanded you, I will tear the kingdom away from you and give it to your servant.” (1 Kings 11:11). Solomon was Israel's king. That's a serious sentence, friends.

The answer is Solomon's servant. The LORD said He would tear the kingdom away from Solomon, Israel's king, and “…give it to your servant.” (1 Kings 11:11). Notice the verse doesn't name the servant. I'll keep my mouth shut where the text keeps its own.

The answer is True, and here's the LORD's own word: “Nevertheless, for the sake of your father David, I will not do it during your lifetime; I will tear it out of the hand of your son.” (1 Kings 11:12). Solomon, Israel's king, hears a hard sentence, and a “nevertheless” comes with it. The reason named is David. I think that one word “nevertheless” is worth underlining, friends.

The answer is one tribe. The LORD says, “I will give one tribe to your son for the sake of My servant David and for the sake of Jerusalem, which I have chosen.” (1 Kings 11:13). Just before that He says He won't tear the whole kingdom away from him. So the son keeps one tribe, friends.

The answer is that it is the city He has chosen, in the LORD's own words. He gives one tribe “…for the sake of My servant David and for the sake of Jerusalem, which I have chosen.” (1 Kings 11:13). Even in a hard speech to Solomon, Israel's king, Jerusalem gets that line. Friends, that's worth a second look.
